doc.title: Dan Wall and Adam Nussbaum interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 19, 2001

title: Original material, Abercrombie as bandleader, and expectations of organ trios
summary: They discuss repertoire in the trio, no label pressure for standards, and audience preconceptions of organ trios.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: You have a pretty good percentage of original material in the trio. Is it a challenge to get your own pieces played these days, other than doing it yourself?

Well the couple of organ records that I’ve done lately I think have been almost all my tunes but maybe a couple of standards. With this band we played some of Adam’s tunes, we played a lot of my tunes which has been really nice, that from the beginning of that, I think the first record was very equal or whatever in the amount of writing. I mean John © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-
basically has always looked for material that we would sound good playing. It doesn’t matter who wrote it. If this works, fine.
That’s good. Do you get pressure from the record people to include standards?
Not with the label that we’ve been involved with.

But a good example, you know that brings up a funny thing though about organ, you know people with preconceived ideas about organ that I have this record out that I think from what I’m hearing the track that’s getting the most airplay—

Yeah, is a standard off the record. Two of ten cuts were standards I think. And one of those standards, because, I mean it works which is great, it has a simple — you know people like hearing standards from the organ and the whole thing. But this band has been very original. The last record we did actually was I think John wrote maybe everything on the record the thing with Lovano and Kenny Wheeler and Mark Feldman. I think there was one track we did a free track.

And there were quite a few free pieces. I mean many people, they look at an organ trio and they think the instrumentation will dictate the conception of the music and oh yeah, man, you guys play a lot of blues or you play a lot of this or a lot of that. Well no we don’t. We just, this is the instrumentation but we have our own approach to how we want to play. And we’ve never really discussed the concept of what we do, we just do it. And we all just listen to each other and whatever happens happens.
